cim_eredeti: Digital Production Channels Artificial Intelligence Capabilities Into Corporate Green Innovation Outcomes
szoveg_eredeti:
Digital Production Channels Artificial Intelligence Capabilities Into Corporate Green Innovation Outcomes

A comprehensive empirical investigation of 275 cross-sector enterprises reveals that artificial intelligence capabilities significantly foster both exploitative and exploratory green innovation, operating both through direct organizational pathways and through the mediating mechanism of digital production. Published in the International Journal of Information Management Data Insights, the structural equation modeling study demonstrates that enterprise-level artificial intelligence competencies exert measurable direct positive effects on incremental green refinements and radical environmental breakthroughs. Furthermore, the empirical findings demonstrate that digital production acts as an indispensable operational harmonizer, partially mediating the relationship between intelligent technological assets and sustainable innovation outcomes. The authors establish that advanced analytical competencies provide the predictive and sensing foundation required for corporate environmental progress, while digitalized operational routines translate those analytical insights into quantifiable resource reductions and sustainable product solutions.

The study grounds its conceptual architecture in organizational ambidexterity theory and the resource-based view, differentiating environmental innovation into two distinct structural orientations: exploitative and exploratory green innovation. Exploitative green innovation focuses on incremental, efficiency-oriented enhancements applied to existing products, operational practices, and manufacturing workflows. Conversely, exploratory green innovation represents a knowledge-intensive orientation centered on radical experimentation and the development of entirely novel environmental solutions. This exploratory mode seeks to transform industry practices by introducing wholly original green products, designing alternative production systems, and utilizing renewable, non-hazardous materials that break fundamentally from established technical baselines. While prior literature documented inherent strategic tensions and resource competition between routine efficiency improvements and uncertain radical experimentation, the investigation illustrates how contemporary computational infrastructures assist organizations in pursuing both sustainability trajectories contemporaneously.

Artificial intelligence capabilities are conceptualized throughout the research not as static software applications, but as high-level organizational competencies that allow companies to acquire, integrate, and deploy sophisticated technologies across core operational functions. These tools encompass machine learning algorithms, deep learning networks, autonomous robotics, computer vision, natural language processing, and predictive analytics. Within organizational settings, these technologies enable automated problem-solving, cognitive reasoning, real-time sensing, and dynamic workflow optimization. The authors emphasize that artificial intelligence operates as a reprogrammable, general-purpose technology capable of analyzing complex operational environments and continuously adapting to changing regulatory frameworks and market demands. Rather than viewing computational adoption as an automatic driver of corporate sustainability, the researchers argue that the strategic value of intelligent systems depends upon their structural alignment with internal management procedures, digital infrastructures, and enterprise-wide green transformation objectives, providing the analytical capacity needed to model alternative lifecycle scenarios and identify hidden inefficiencies.

To explain how analytical intelligence translates into practical environmental achievements, the researchers examine digital production as an active operational mechanism rather than an inert technological asset. Digital production refers to an integrated operational system that deploys advanced information technologies, Internet of Things sensors, automated workflows, and algorithmic coordination to maximize system flexibility, precision, and operational transparency. In manufacturing environments, digital production facilitates predictive maintenance schedules, automated energy monitoring, closed-loop material recycling, and digital twin modeling. In service environments, the construct manifests through algorithmic decision support, data-driven workflow routing, and intelligent service automation. The structural framework posits that digital production establishes a complementary technological bridge: artificial intelligence algorithms analyze the rich operational data streams generated across digital networks, while the flexible execution capabilities of digital production systems implement algorithmic insights directly into day-to-day operations, establishing a synchronized organizational learning cycle that reduces operational waste and shortens sustainable development cycles.

The empirical evaluation utilized a rigorous multi-stage survey methodology to gather data from corporate leaders and senior managers across three primary industrial sectors. The initial survey instrument underwent extensive pretesting, including content validity assessments drawn from academic literature and structured reviews by seven academic specialists in artificial intelligence, digital production, and sustainable innovation. The research team deployed purposive sampling across enterprises known to have implemented artificial intelligence initiatives and corporate sustainability strategies, identifying targets through sustainability reports and official documentation. Out of 500 distributed questionnaires, 283 were retrieved, and 275 complete responses were retained following data screening, yielding an effective response rate of 55 percent. The demographic composition comprised 168 small and medium-sized enterprises representing 61.1 percent of the sample and 107 large enterprises accounting for 38.9 percent. Across industries, manufacturing firms represented 42.9 percent with 118 organizations, technology companies constituted 31.3 percent with 86 organizations, and service enterprises comprised 25.8 percent with 71 organizations. In terms of digital maturity, 23.3 percent reported low maturity, 44.0 percent medium maturity, and 32.7 percent high maturity.

Measurement validation was executed within SmartPLS 4, evaluating internal consistency, convergent validity, and discriminant validity across all multi-item constructs based on five-point Likert scales. The remaining indicators exhibited satisfactory psychometric performance, with all item loadings exceeding 0.70 and variance inflation factors remaining well below the conservative threshold of 5. For artificial intelligence capabilities, Cronbach’s alpha reached 0.93, composite reliability reached 0.95, and average variance extracted reached 0.82. Digital production achieved a Cronbach’s alpha of 0.89, composite reliability of 0.92, and average variance extracted of 0.75. Exploitative green innovation recorded a Cronbach’s alpha of 0.88, composite reliability of 0.92, and average variance extracted of 0.79, while exploratory green innovation demonstrated a Cronbach’s alpha of 0.91, composite reliability of 0.94, and average variance extracted of 0.84. Discriminant validity was fully supported by both Fornell-Larcker criterion evaluations and Heterotrait-Monotrait ratio tests.

Before conducting final hypothesis testing, the researchers completed robust diagnostic evaluations to rule out potential non-response bias, common method bias, and structural endogeneity.
